text: And here's the part that stings. Years before the iPhone, Nokia had a touchscreen phone with the internet on it. Working. In a lab.
I'm Sam. This is Last Receipt. Tonight, the rise and fall of Nokia.
Here's the thing about Nokia. It had already reinvented itself completely, once. That should have been its superpower.
Think about that. One company, in a country of about five million people, made about four in every ten phones on Earth.
Now watch this. Management looked at it and said no. It would be expensive to make. It might not sell. And Nokia was making plenty of money with the phones it already had.
That's the trap. The year your replacement arrives is often your best year ever. The numbers tell you you're winning, right up until they don't.
Funny thing. Lego's boss used the same phrase a few years earlier, and it saved Lego. The difference was where they jumped.
The company that made boots, then cables, then phones, has reinvented itself again. It just lost the phones along the way.
So what killed Nokia's phone business? The iPhone. Android. Windows. All true.
But Nokia had a touchscreen phone with the internet years early, and it put it in a drawer because the old phones were still selling so well.
Then, when it finally jumped, it jumped to the wrong platform.
The lesson: the moment you're selling more than ever is the moment to ask what will replace you. And if the answer is already in your lab, ship it.
